statement: The /goal command requires Claude Code v2.1.139 or later, sets one completion condition per session, and clears itself automatically once the condition is met.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+ (interactive, headless -p, desktop, Remote Control)
candidate_guidance: Treat v2.1.139 as the floor before any repo guidance recommends /goal. Do not assume more than one concurrent goal per session; a second /goal replaces the first.

reason: Every element verified verbatim on the tier-1 page. Version floor: 'Note: /goal requires Claude Code v2.1.139 or later.' Concurrency: 'One goal can be active per session.' Replacement: 'If a goal is already active, the new one replaces it.' Auto-clear: 'The goal clears automatically once the condition is met.' Applicability also holds: 'Setting a goal with -p runs the loop to completion in a single invocation' and /goal 'works in non-interactive mode, in the desktop app, and through Remote Control.'

statement: /goal is implemented as a wrapper around a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook: after each turn the condition plus the conversation are sent to the configured small fast model (default Haiku), which returns a yes/no decision and a short reason that is fed back as guidance for the next turn.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+
candidate_guidance: This is the mechanism to cite when explaining why /goal is unavailable under hook restrictions and why evaluation cost is billed separately on the small fast model. A hand-written Stop hook is the escape hatch when the evaluator needs deterministic (script) checks instead of model judgement.

sources.title: Keep Claude working toward a goal

reason: The 'How evaluation works' section states it almost word for word: '/goal is a wrapper around a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook. Each time Claude finishes a turn, the condition and the conversation so far are sent to your configured small fast model, which defaults to Haiku. The model returns a yes-or-no decision and a short reason. A "no" tells Claude to keep working and includes the reason as guidance for the next turn.' Billing element of the guidance is also supported: 'Evaluation tokens are billed on the small fast model configured for your provider and are typically negligible compared to main-turn spend.' The Stop-hook escape hatch is documented in the See-also block: 'Prompt-based hooks: write your own Stop hook when you need custom evaluation logic', and the comparison table notes a Stop hook 'can run a script for deterministic checks or a prompt for model-evaluated ones.'

statement: The /goal evaluator does not call tools; it can only judge what Claude has already surfaced in the conversation transcript.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+
candidate_guidance: Highest-leverage constraint in this bucket. Any goal condition must be written so the agent's own transcript output demonstrates it (e.g. 'npm test exits 0' with the run visible), otherwise the evaluator is judging an assertion rather than evidence. This is the loop-level analogue of the repo's existing finding that self-authored checks are weaker than diff-derived oracles.

sources.title: Keep Claude working toward a goal

reason: Stated twice on the page. In 'How evaluation works': 'It does not call tools, so it can only judge what Claude has already surfaced in the conversation.' And in 'Write an effective condition': 'The evaluator judges your condition against what Claude has surfaced in the conversation. It doesn't run commands or read files independently, so write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate.' The doc even supplies the same worked example the guidance uses: '"All tests in test/auth pass" works because Claude runs the tests and the result lands in the transcript for the evaluator to read.' The guidance's recommended condition shape is also documented directly ('A stated check: how Claude should prove it, such as "npm test exits 0"').

statement: A /goal condition can be up to 4,000 characters, and there is no separate turn-limit flag: bounding a goal's runtime is done by writing a turn or time clause into the condition text itself (for example 'or stop after 20 turns'), which the evaluator judges from the conversation.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+
candidate_guidance: Note the asymmetry with the Agent SDK, which has real max_turns/max_budget_usd ceilings. /goal's bound is model-judged, not enforced by the harness, so a runaway /goal is bounded only by the evaluator's cooperation plus manual Ctrl+C or /goal clear. Recommend pairing /goal with an SDK-level or wrapper-level hard ceiling for unattended use.

reason: Character limit verbatim: 'The condition can be up to 4,000 characters.' Bounding mechanism verbatim: 'To bound how long a goal runs, include a turn or time clause in the condition, such as "or stop after 20 turns". Claude reports progress against that clause each turn and the evaluator judges it from the conversation.' The 'no separate turn-limit flag' element is an absence claim: I read the full /goal page and found no flag, setting, or env var for a turn or budget ceiling; the doc presents the in-condition clause as the way to bound a goal, and the only documented hard stops are '/goal clear' and Ctrl+C ('Interrupt the process with Ctrl+C to stop a non-interactive goal'). The SDK asymmetry in the guidance is independently confirmed: the agent-loop page gives max_turns/maxTurns and max_budget_usd/maxBudgetUsd as real harness-enforced ceilings. statement: /goal is unavailable in untrusted workspaces, when disableAllHooks is set at any settings level, or when allowManagedHooksOnly is set in managed settings; the command reports the reason rather than silently doing nothing.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+; enterprise/managed-settings environments
candidate_guidance: Relevant for any repo guidance that assumes /goal is universally available. In locked-down orgs the fallback is an explicitly managed Stop hook or SDK-level max_turns, not /goal.

In each case, the command tells you why instead of silently doing nothing.' All three unavailability conditions plus the reports-the-reason behavior match exactly.

statement: An active goal is restored when a session is resumed with --resume or --continue, but the turn count, timer, and token-spend baseline all reset on resume; an already-achieved or cleared goal is not restored.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+
candidate_guidance: Means a 'stop after N turns' clause silently re-arms across resumes, so a resumed goal can consume far more than the intended budget. Flag this in any long-running-session recipe.

The condition carries over, but the turn count, timer, and token-spend baseline all reset on resume. A goal that was already achieved or cleared is not restored.' The guidance's inference that a 'stop after N turns' clause silently re-arms across resumes follows directly from the documented turn-count reset combined with claim -04's in-condition bounding, and is a sound derivation rather than a documented sentence.

statement: /loop behavior is determined by what is supplied: interval plus prompt runs on a fixed cron schedule; prompt only runs at a Claude-chosen interval between one minute and one hour picked after each iteration; interval only or nothing runs the built-in maintenance prompt or a loop.md if one exists.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x (bundled /loop skill); different on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry
candidate_guidance: Use this three-way table verbatim when documenting /loop. Note the provider caveat: on Bedrock/AWS/GCP/Foundry a prompt with no interval runs on a fixed 10-minute schedule, and bare /loop prints usage instead of running the maintenance prompt.

statement: A loop.md file replaces the built-in maintenance prompt for bare /loop; Claude reads .claude/loop.md (project scope, takes precedence) then ~/.claude/loop.md (user scope), edits take effect on the next iteration, and content beyond 25,000 bytes is truncated.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x; not read on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry
candidate_guidance: This is the checked-in, reviewable place to encode a repo's default maintenance loop. The 25,000-byte truncation is a hard budget worth stating explicitly. Note loop.md defines a single default prompt, not a list of scheduled tasks.

statement: In self-paced /loop mode Claude ends the loop by calling the ScheduleWakeup tool with stop: true, which cancels the pending wakeup immediately; if an iteration ends without either rescheduling or stopping, Claude Code schedules one fallback wakeup about 20 minutes later and ends the loop when that iteration also fails to reschedule. Before v2.1.202, not rescheduling was the only way Claude could end a loop on its own.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.202+ for the stop: true path; earlier versions self-terminate only by omitting a reschedule
candidate_guidance: This is the actual termination primitive for self-paced loops and the single most citable mechanic in this bucket. The ~20-minute fallback wakeup means an apparently finished loop still costs one more iteration; budget for it.

Before v2.1.202, not rescheduling was the only way Claude could end a loop on its own.' statement: Session-scoped scheduling uses three tools, CronCreate, CronList, and CronDelete, accepting standard 5-field cron expressions interpreted in local time; each task has an 8-character ID and a session can hold at most 50 scheduled tasks at once.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x, in-session (not Routines or Desktop scheduled tasks)
candidate_guidance: Quote the 50-task ceiling and the 8-character ID when writing orchestration guidance. Extended cron syntax (L, W, ?, MON/JAN aliases) is explicitly unsupported; when both day-of-month and day-of-week are constrained, a date matches if either matches (vixie-cron semantics).

sources.title: Run prompts on a schedule

reason: Tool table confirms CronCreate ('Accepts a 5-field cron expression, the prompt to run, and whether it recurs or fires once'), CronList, and CronDelete. Ceilings verbatim: 'Each scheduled task has an 8-character ID you can pass to CronDelete. A session can hold up to 50 scheduled tasks at once.' Timezone verbatim: 'All times are interpreted in your local timezone. A cron expression like 0 9 * * * means 9am wherever you're running Claude Code, not UTC.' Both guidance details confirmed in the cron reference: 'Extended syntax like L, W, ?, and name aliases such as MON or JAN is not supported' and 'When both day-of-month and day-of-week are constrained, a date matches if either field matches. This follows standard vixie-cron semantics.'

statement: Recurring session-scoped scheduled tasks automatically expire 7 days after creation: the task fires one final time and then deletes itself, and this expiry also applies to dynamically scheduled (self-paced) loops.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x, in-session scheduling only
candidate_guidance: This is the built-in blast-radius bound on a forgotten loop. Any guidance recommending durable automation should point at Routines, Desktop scheduled tasks, or GitHub Actions rather than expecting a /loop to persist past a week.

statement: The scheduler applies deterministic jitter derived from the task ID: recurring tasks fire up to 30 minutes after the scheduled time (or up to half the interval for sub-hourly tasks), and one-shot tasks scheduled for the top or bottom of the hour fire up to 90 seconds early.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x, in-session scheduling
candidate_guidance: Concrete workaround worth recording: pick a minute other than :00 or :30 (for example '3 9 * * *') and the one-shot jitter does not apply. Do not design cross-system handoffs that assume exact fire times.

sources.title: Run prompts on a schedule

Determinism confirmed: 'The offset is derived from the task ID, so the same task always gets the same offset.' The guidance's workaround is the doc's own: 'If exact timing matters, pick a minute that is not :00 or :30, for example 3 9 * * * instead of 0 9 * * *, and the one-shot jitter will not apply.'

statement: Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CRON=1 in the environment disables the scheduler entirely: the cron tools and /loop become unavailable and already-scheduled tasks stop firing.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x
candidate_guidance: The kill switch for in-session scheduling. Useful for CI images and locked-down agent runners where an autonomous loop must be impossible rather than merely discouraged.

statement: As of Claude Code v2.1.196, a scheduled fire only executes skills that Claude is allowed to invoke on its own; built-in commands such as /permissions, /model, or /clear, skills marked disable-model-invocation: true, skills withheld by a skillOverrides setting or a Skill deny rule, and MCP prompts all reach Claude as plain text instead of executing.

candidate_guidance: Directly determines whether '/loop 20m /my-skill' actually runs the skill. Any repo skill intended for scheduled use must remain model-invocable; check its frontmatter and any skillOverrides or Skill deny rules before relying on it in a loop.

The endpoint ships under the experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01 beta header.

candidate_guidance: This is the prompt-injection boundary for externally triggered loops and matches the repo's instruction-source rule: fire text is data, not instructions. Anyone holding the bearer token can send text, so the wrapper is the containment. Breaking changes ship behind new dated beta headers with the two most recent previous versions still working.

statement: Routines run autonomously as full Claude Code cloud sessions with no permission-mode picker and no approval prompts during a run; by default Claude can only push to branches prefixed with claude/, unless 'Allow unrestricted branch pushes' is enabled for that repository.
applicability: Claude Code Routines research preview, July 2026
candidate_guidance: The blast radius of a routine is set entirely at configuration time by repositories, branch-push setting, environment network access and variables, and included connectors. All connected MCP connectors are included by default and Claude may use every tool from them including writes, so pruning connectors is the main least-privilege lever.

statement: The Agent SDK caps the loop with max_turns / maxTurns (counting tool-use round trips only) and max_budget_usd / maxBudgetUsd; both default to no limit, and hitting either returns a ResultMessage with subtype error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd, on which the result text field is absent.
applicability: Claude Agent SDK (Python and TypeScript), July 2026
candidate_guidance: These are the only hard, harness-enforced ceilings in the Claude loop family. Always check ResultMessage.subtype before reading result. All subtypes still carry total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns, and session_id, so a truncated run can be resumed with a higher limit rather than restarted.

statement: A single-shot query() that ends on an error result yields the final result message and then raises/throws (the Claude Code process also exits nonzero), whereas a streaming-input session stays alive and can keep receiving messages.
applicability: Claude Agent SDK (Python and TypeScript), July 2026
candidate_guidance: Practical harness detail: wrap single-shot query() in try/except or try/catch or a max-turns stop will surface as an unhandled exception rather than a clean budget exhaustion. Choose streaming input when the harness needs to survive a ceiling hit.

sources.title: How the agent loop works

reason: The note under 'Handle the result' states all three elements verbatim: 'A single-shot query() call yields the final result message, then raises an error that includes the failure text, such as "Reached maximum number of turns". The raise is intentional - wrap the loop in a try block if your code needs to continue past it. The underlying Claude Code process also exits with a nonzero code.' and 'A streaming input session stays alive, and you can keep sending messages.' The guidance's try/except recommendation is the doc's own, and its worked examples wrap query() in try blocks for exactly this reason. One refinement for implementers: the doc notes connection or process failures yield no result message at all, so the except branch cannot assume a result was seen.

statement: The Monitor tool streams background script output or WebSocket events back into a running session instead of polling, uses the same permission rules as Bash for commands, and is unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, and when DISABLE_TELEMETRY or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set. Its WebSocket source requires Claude Code v2.1.195 or later.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x; WebSocket source v2.1.195+
candidate_guidance: The docs state Monitor is often more token-efficient and responsive than re-running a prompt on an interval, so prefer it over /loop for pure watch-and-react work. WebSocket watches end on socket close, on any message larger than 1 MiB, and take a ws input (url required, protocols optional) that cannot be combined with command; private, link-local, and cloud-metadata addresses are denied.

statement: Claude Code v2.1.212 (July 17, 2026) added two per-session runaway-loop ceilings: a cap on subagent spawns per session (default 200, override with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION, reset by /clear) explicitly to stop runaway delegation loops, and a session-wide WebSearch tool-call limit (default 200, tunable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION) explicitly to stop runaway search loops.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.x (July 2026 changelog); exact introducing version uncertain, see open questions

Two independent tier-1 reads agree: the hosted changelog and the canonical anthropics/claude-code CHANGELOG.md both place both entries under 2.1.212, so the earlier v2.1.199 reading was wrong. Cite the env var names and the 200 defaults as documented. Note these are usage-count circuit breakers, not turn or budget ceilings: neither bounds turns or spend the way the SDK's max_turns/max_budget_usd do, so they narrow but do not close the CLI-vs-SDK asymmetry recorded in claim -04.

statement: In claude -p runs, background Bash tasks are terminated about five seconds after the final result and stdin closes, while background subagents and workflows are waited for; from v2.1.182 that wait is capped at ten minutes by default, adjustable with CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS or set to 0 to wait without a limit.
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.182+ in non-interactive (-p) mode
candidate_guidance: Essential for scripted/CI harnesses: a stuck background agent can no longer hold a -p invocation open indefinitely, but ten minutes of dead wait is still charged wall-clock time. SIGTERM aborts the turn, kills the Bash process tree, runs SessionEnd hooks, and exits 143.

statement: Claude Code documents three distinct ways to keep a session running between prompts, differing in what starts the next turn and what stops it: /goal (next turn starts when the previous finishes; stops when a model confirms the condition), /loop (next turn starts when a time interval elapses; stops when you stop it or Claude decides the work is done), and a Stop hook (fires after every turn; your own script or prompt decides).
applicability: Claude Code CLI v2.1.139+ for /goal; v2.1.x for /loop and Stop hooks
candidate_guidance: This trigger/terminator table is the cleanest framing for a repo decision rule. Key distinction to preserve: /goal is session-scoped and typed at the prompt, whereas a Stop hook lives in settings, applies to every session in its scope, and can run a deterministic script rather than a model judgement.

statement: Anthropic's harness-design engineering write-up (March 24, 2026) distinguishes context resets - 'clearing the context window entirely and starting a fresh agent, combined with a structured handoff that carries the previous agent's state and the next steps' - from compaction, where 'earlier parts of the conversation are summarized in place so the same agent can keep going on a shortened history.' It reports that Claude Sonnet 4.5 'exhibited context anxiety strongly enough that compaction alone wasn't sufficient to enable strong long task performance, so context resets became essential,' whereas Opus 4.5 'largely removed that behavior on its own, so I was able to drop context resets from this harness entirely.'

candidate_guidance: Model-version open question is now RESOLVED by direct read: Sonnet 4.5 is the model that needed context resets; Opus 4.5 is the release that removed the need. Opus 4.6 is mentioned separately in the article as a later release ('plans more carefully, sustains agentic tasks for longer') and is NOT the model credited with eliminating context anxiety - that was the source of the earlier confusion. The transferable lesson is the article's own meta-point, quotable directly: 'every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be incorrect, and because they can quickly go stale as models improve.' This is the strongest external corroboration available for the repo's own null results on adaptive-mode scaffolding, and it argues for re-measuring whether each scaffolding step still earns its place. Separately, reclassify this claim as version_sensitive: false - it is an account of a fixed, dated publication, not a product behavior that ships with a CLI release.

statement: A Claude Code hook that exits with code 2 signals a blocking error: Claude Code ignores the hook's stdout (including any JSON it printed) and feeds the hook's stderr text back to Claude as the error message.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, command-type hooks (verified against docs at CHANGELOG v2.1.215)
candidate_guidance: Policy-enforcing hooks should `exit 2` with the human-readable reason on stderr. Never print structured JSON and exit 2 in the same run - the docs state explicitly that JSON is ignored on exit 2, so the two control channels must not be mixed.

reason: Verbatim in the reference: 'Exit 2 means a blocking error. Claude Code ignores stdout and any JSON in it. Instead, stderr text is fed back to Claude as an error message.' Exit 0 is the only code where 'Claude Code parses stdout for JSON output fields.' The guide carries the matching Note: 'Use exit 2 to block with a stderr message, or exit 0 with JSON for structured control. Don't mix them: Claude Code ignores JSON when you exit 2.' The candidate guidance's do-not-mix instruction is the docs' own wording. Corroborating signal in the changelog ('Fixed hooks with exit code 2 not blocking as documented when the hook's stdout JSON fails schema validation') reinforces that the two channels are separate.

statement: Exit code 1, and any non-zero exit code other than 2, is treated as a NON-blocking error for hook events: the action proceeds, the transcript shows a `<hook name> hook error` notice followed by the first line of stderr, and full stderr goes to the debug log. The documented exception is `WorktreeCreate`, where any non-zero exit code fails worktree creation.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, command-type hooks
candidate_guidance: This is the highest-value trap in the whole bucket: a guard script that follows Unix convention and exits 1 on policy violation FAILS OPEN. Any hook intended to enforce a rule must be audited so that every rejection path exits exactly 2. The docs carry their own warning about this.

statement: The converse of hook-deny precedence does not hold: a PreToolUse hook returning `permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the interactive prompt but does not override deny rules from any settings scope including managed settings, does not suppress explicit `ask` rules, and does not suppress prompts for connector tools an organization set to `ask` or MCP tools marked `requiresUserInteraction`.

statement: For most hook events a `matcher` is evaluated three different ways: `"*"`, `""`, or an omitted matcher matches everything; a value containing only letters, digits, underscore, hyphen, spaces, comma and pipe is treated as an exact name or a list of exact names; a value containing any other character is compiled as an unanchored JavaScript regex (tested with `RegExp.prototype.test`, so it matches anywhere in the value). Matchers are case-sensitive. Two events are exceptions: `FileChanged` and `StopFailure` use a narrower exact-match set of letters, digits, `_` and `|` only, so a hyphen, space or comma in a matcher for those two events keeps it on the regular-expression path and only `|` separates alternatives.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, hook matcher field
candidate_guidance: The unanchored-regex rule is the sharp edge: a matcher like `Bash.*` is regex and matches broadly (`Edit.*` matches both `Edit` and `NotebookEdit`), while `Bash` is an exact match. If you intend a prefix match, write the regex deliberately and anchor it (e.g. `^Notebook`); if you intend exact matching, keep the value free of regex metacharacters, and anchor as `^name$` when you need a whole-string match. Do not reuse a hyphen-, space-, or comma-containing matcher pattern from a tool event on `FileChanged` or `StopFailure` — those two events apply a narrower exact-match character set, so the same string silently switches to regex evaluation there.

reason: Numbers match both pages exactly. Reference common-fields: 'Defaults: 600 for `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool`; 30 for `prompt`; 60 for `agent`. UserPromptSubmit lowers the `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool` default to 30, and MessageDisplay lowers it to 10.' The guide's Limitations restates the same figures in minutes ('`command`, `http`, `mcp_tool`: 10 minutes. UserPromptSubmit lowers these to 30 seconds, and MessageDisplay lowers them to 10 seconds. `prompt`: 30 seconds. `agent`: 60 seconds'). Guidance is sound: `timeout` is documented as per-handler customizable, and a hung PreToolUse guard on the 600s default would stall the turn.

statement: Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress; hook scripts are expected to read the `stop_hook_active` field from their JSON input and exit 0 when it is true, and the cap can be raised with the `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP` environment variable.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, Stop and SubagentStop hooks
candidate_guidance: Any Stop-hook-driven verification loop needs the `stop_hook_active` early-exit or it will burn eight extra model turns before the harness cuts it off. Treat the cap as a safety net, not a design parameter.

sources.title: Automate actions with hooks - Claude Code Docs

reason: The guide's 'Stop hook hits the block cap' troubleshooting section supports all three parts: 'Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress. Your hook script needs to check whether it already triggered a continuation. Parse the `stop_hook_active` field from the JSON input and exit early if it's `true`', with a bash example that exits 0 on true. And: 'If your hook legitimately needs more than eight iterations to converge, raise the cap with `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`.' The candidate guidance follows directly.

statement: PermissionRequest hooks do not fire in non-interactive mode with the `-p` flag; the documented substitute for automated permission decisions in headless runs is a PreToolUse hook.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, headless/-p sessions
candidate_guidance: Any CI or scripted pipeline that relies on PermissionRequest auto-approval will silently lose that control in headless mode. Port such logic to PreToolUse before moving a workflow from interactive to `-p`.

sources.title: Automate actions with hooks - Claude Code Docs

reason: Stated twice in the guide. Limitations: '`PermissionRequest` hooks don't fire in non-interactive mode with the `-p` flag. Use `PreToolUse` hooks for automated permission decisions.' Repeated in the 'Hook not firing' troubleshooting list: 'If using `PermissionRequest` hooks in non-interactive mode with the `-p` flag, switch to `PreToolUse` instead.' The claim's port-before-you-migrate guidance is exactly the documented substitute.

statement: In auto mode each action goes through a fixed decision order where the first matching step wins: (1) actions matching allow, ask or deny rules resolve immediately — except that writes to protected paths route to the classifier even when an allow rule matches, connector tools an organization set to `ask` and MCP tools marked `requiresUserInteraction` prompt the user directly even when an allow rule matches, and content-scoped ask rules fall back to a permission prompt; (2) read-only actions and file edits in the working directory are auto-approved, except writes to protected paths; (3) everything else goes to the classifier; (4) if the classifier blocks, Claude receives the reason and tries an alternative.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode
candidate_guidance: This is the canonical statement of deny-before-classifier: a `permissions.deny` rule resolves at step 1 and the classifier is never consulted, so deterministic denial always wins over the probabilistic layer. The converse does not hold symmetrically — an allow rule does not universally short-circuit the classifier, because protected-path writes are routed to the classifier even with a matching allow rule, and org `ask` connector tools and `requiresUserInteraction` MCP tools prompt regardless. When placing a control, treat rule evaluation as strictly upstream for blocking, but never assume an allow rule is sufficient to guarantee an action runs without a classifier round-trip or a prompt.

reason: The four-step skeleton and the 'The first matching step wins' framing are verbatim in the permission-modes accordion 'How the classifier evaluates actions', and the deny-before-classifier conclusion is independently confirmed by auto-mode-config ('permissions.deny | Blocks before the classifier is consulted. Neither the classifier nor user intent can override it'). Corrected because the claim's step 1 reproduces only the headline sentence and drops three qualifiers the docs attach to it in the same breath — most importantly 'Writes to protected paths route to the classifier even when an allow rule matches.' That omission is what makes the original candidate_guidance ('deterministic controls always win over the probabilistic layer') too strong as written: it is true of deny, false of allow. Since this claim was explicitly framed as the canonical mental model for where to place a control, shipping the unqualified version would license the wrong inference that an allow rule reliably keeps an action away from the classifier. Claim 29 independently confirms the protected-path carve-out, so the two claims must not contradict each other in the same contract.

statement: `permissions.deny` rules block an action before the auto mode classifier is consulted and cannot be overridden by classifier configuration or by user intent stated in conversation; the `autoMode` prose rule lists are a second gate that runs after the permissions system.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode with managed or user settings
candidate_guidance: For anything that must never run regardless of user intent, the docs direct you to `permissions.deny` in managed settings rather than to an `autoMode.hard_deny` entry. Reserve autoMode prose rules for shaping classifier judgement, not for hard policy.

reason: Both halves are verbatim in auto-mode-config. The boundary table: 'Never run the action | `permissions.deny` | Blocks before the classifier is consulted. Neither the classifier nor user intent can override it.' The second-gate framing, in a Note: 'The classifier is a second gate that runs after the permissions system. For actions that must never run regardless of user intent or classifier configuration, use `permissions.deny` in managed settings, which blocks the action before the classifier is consulted and can't be overridden.' That Note is also the source of the candidate guidance, near word for word. The page's opening paragraph corroborates: 'Deny and explicit ask rules are evaluated before the classifier and still block or prompt.'

statement: Entering auto mode drops broad allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution - blanket `Bash(*)` or `PowerShell(*)`, wildcarded interpreters such as `Bash(python*)`, package-manager run commands, and `Agent` allow rules - and restores them when the session leaves auto mode; narrow rules such as `Bash(npm test)` carry over and resolve before the classifier runs.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode
candidate_guidance: A narrow carried-over rule can still let a destructive argument through without the classifier ever seeing it, because rule matching is upstream of the classifier. Where that matters, set `autoMode.classifyAllShell: true` to force every shell command through the classifier.

reason: Verbatim in the permission-modes classifier accordion: 'On entering auto mode, broad allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution are dropped: Blanket `Bash(*)` or `PowerShell(*)`; Wildcarded interpreters like `Bash(python*)`; Package-manager run commands; `Agent` allow rules. Narrow rules like `Bash(npm test)` carry over. Dropped rules are restored when you leave auto mode.' The four dropped categories, the carry-over of narrow rules, and the restoration on exit all match exactly. The guidance's escape-hatch reasoning is the docs' own, from auto-mode-config: 'a narrow rule can still let a destructive argument through without the classifier seeing it, for example a script path or flag the rule's prefix didn't anticipate', which that page then answers with `autoMode.classifyAllShell` — consistent with claim 30.

statement: The auto mode classifier is reasoning-blind by design: it sees user messages, tool calls, and CLAUDE.md content, while Claude's own messages and all tool results are stripped, so hostile content arriving in a file or web page cannot address the classifier directly. A separate server-side probe scans incoming tool results and flags suspicious content before Claude reads it.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode classifier
candidate_guidance: This is the architectural reason the classifier resists prompt injection, and also the reason it cannot verify a value that only exists in command output - which is why auto mode blocks recursive deletes whose target is an unresolved shell variable. Injection defense and blind spots come from the same design choice.

reason: Confirmed by two independent tier-1 sources, including the part the docs page alone would not have settled. permission-modes: 'The classifier sees user messages, tool calls, and your CLAUDE.md content. Tool results are stripped, so hostile content in a file or web page cannot manipulate it directly. A separate server-side probe scans incoming tool results and flags suspicious content before Claude reads it.' The claim's additional assertion that Claude's own messages are stripped — which permission-modes implies only by omission — is stated outright in the engineering post: the classifier sees 'only user messages and the agent's tool calls; we strip out Claude's own messages and tool outputs', with the rationale 'We strip assistant text so the agent can't talk the classifier into making a bad call.' The post also confirms the probe: 'a server-side prompt-injection probe scans tool outputs (file reads, web fetches, shell output, external tool responses) before they enter the agent's context.' The guidance's blind-spot corollary is independently verified by the v2.1.205 default block rule on permission-modes, which blocks `rm -rf "$VAR"` whose target is unassigned in the visible conversation because 'The classifier reads the conversation rather than command output by design.' Note the claim wisely asserts no classifier model — the engineering post still says Sonnet 4.6 while permission-modes documents a Sonnet 5 default from v2.1.210, so any claim naming the model would have been stale.

statement: If the auto mode classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times total, auto mode pauses and Claude Code resumes prompting; these thresholds are not configurable. Any allowed action resets the consecutive counter while the total counter persists for the session. In non-interactive mode with `-p`, repeated blocks abort the session because there is no user to prompt.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode
candidate_guidance: Treat repeated denials as a signal that the classifier lacks environment context rather than as a reason to loosen rules. In headless pipelines this becomes a hard abort, so an unconfigured `autoMode.environment` turns into pipeline flakiness.

reason: permission-modes, 'When auto mode falls back': 'If the classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times total, auto mode pauses and Claude Code resumes prompting. Approving the prompted action resumes auto mode. These thresholds are not configurable. Any allowed action resets the consecutive counter, while the total counter persists for the session and resets only when its own limit triggers a fallback.' And: 'In non-interactive mode with the `-p` flag, repeated blocks abort the session since there is no user to prompt.' The engineering post independently confirms the numbers ('If a session accumulates 3 consecutive denials or 20 total, we stop the model and escalate to the human'). One immaterial nuance: the claim says the total counter 'persists for the session' and omits the docs' trailing clause that it resets when its own limit triggers a fallback — not false, just less complete, and it does not affect the guidance. The guidance's advice to treat repeated denials as missing environment context rather than a reason to loosen rules is the docs' own framing.

statement: Auto mode block-lists are customised through four array-of-prose settings keys: `autoMode.environment`, `autoMode.allow`, `autoMode.soft_deny` and `autoMode.hard_deny`. Including the literal string `"$defaults"` in an array splices the built-in list in at that position; omitting it replaces that section's built-in rules entirely.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `autoMode` settings block
candidate_guidance: Omitting `"$defaults"` is a silent, high-blast-radius mistake: setting `soft_deny` without it discards every built-in soft block including force push, `curl | bash`, production deploys and auto-mode bypass, and setting `hard_deny` without it discards the built-in data-exfiltration rule. Always include `"$defaults"` unless deliberately taking full ownership of a list.

sources.title: Configure auto mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: All four keys are documented as prose arrays ('Each is an array of prose descriptions, read as natural-language rules'; for environment, 'Entries are prose, not regex or tool patterns'). Splice semantics verbatim: 'To keep the built-in rules while adding your own, include the literal string "$defaults" in the array. The default rules are spliced in at that position, so your custom rules can go before or after them.' The omission consequence is a Danger callout that names exactly the losses the guidance cites: 'Setting any of `environment`, `allow`, `soft_deny`, or `hard_deny` without "$defaults" replaces the entire default list for that section... `soft_deny`: every built-in soft block rule, including force push, `curl | bash`, production deploys, and auto-mode bypass; `hard_deny`: the built-in data exfiltration rule.' Also confirmed that sections are independent ('setting `environment` alone leaves the default `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` lists intact'), which sharpens the blast radius to the edited section only.

statement: Inside the classifier, rule precedence works in four tiers: `hard_deny` blocks unconditionally and neither user intent nor `allow` exceptions apply; `soft_deny` blocks next; `allow` entries then override matching `soft_deny` rules; and explicit, specific user intent overrides the remaining soft blocks. Because scopes combine additively, a developer-added `allow` entry can override an organization `soft_deny` entry, so `autoMode` is not a hard policy boundary.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `autoMode` settings across user and managed scopes
candidate_guidance: An organization that needs a boundary a developer cannot lift must use `permissions.deny` in managed settings or `autoMode.hard_deny`, not `soft_deny`. General requests do not count as explicit intent - the docs contrast 'clean up the repo' (does not authorize a force push) with 'force-push this branch' (does).

sources.title: Configure auto mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: The four tiers are a verbatim bulleted list: '`hard_deny` rules block unconditionally. User intent and `allow` exceptions don't apply. `soft_deny` rules block next. User intent and `allow` exceptions can override these. `allow` rules then override matching `soft_deny` rules as exceptions. Explicit user intent overrides the remaining soft blocks.' The additive-scope conclusion is equally explicit: 'A developer can extend `environment`, `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` with personal entries but can't remove entries that managed settings provide. Because allow rules act as exceptions to soft block rules inside the classifier, a developer-added `allow` entry can override an organization `soft_deny` entry: the combination is additive, not a hard policy boundary.' The intent example matches word for word: 'Asking Claude to "clean up the repo" doesn't authorize force-pushing, but asking Claude to "force-push this branch" does.' The guidance's claim that hard_deny is also a viable org boundary holds under this page's own logic: managed entries cannot be removed by a developer, and allow exceptions do not apply to hard_deny.

statement: The classifier does not read the `autoMode` block from `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json` - only from `~/.claude/settings.json`, managed settings, or inline JSON via the `--settings` flag or Agent SDK - so a checked-in repository or a build step cannot inject its own allow rules. Before v2.1.207 the classifier also read `.claude/settings.local.json`.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.207+ (project-local exclusion), `autoMode` settings block
candidate_guidance: If an `autoMode` block appears to have no effect, check which file it lives in before debugging the rules themselves. Repos that shipped an `autoMode` block in `.claude/settings.local.json` under an older client need it moved to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

sources.title: Configure auto mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: Verbatim: 'The classifier doesn't read `autoMode` from project settings in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`. Both files live in the repo directory, so a checked-in repo or a build step could otherwise inject its own allow rules. Before v2.1.207, the classifier also read `.claude/settings.local.json`; move any `autoMode` block in that file to `~/.claude/settings.json`.' The permitted scopes match the claim exactly, per the page's scope table: `~/.claude/settings.json`, managed settings, and `--settings` flag or Agent SDK inline JSON. The trust-boundary rationale and the migration instruction in the candidate guidance are both the docs' own.

statement: Claude Code v2.1.142 and later ignore `permissions.defaultMode: "auto"` when it is set in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`, so a repository cannot grant itself auto mode; the setting must live in `~/.claude/settings.json` (or managed settings) to take effect.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.142+, `permissions.defaultMode` setting
candidate_guidance: A session that starts in `default` mode with no error despite `defaultMode: "auto"` in settings is almost always this rule firing. Same trust-boundary principle as the `autoMode` scope exclusion: repo-controlled files cannot escalate their own privileges.

sources.title: Choose a permission mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: Verbatim, including the diagnostic symptom the guidance leans on: 'If you set `defaultMode: "auto"` in settings and the session starts in `default` mode with no error, the setting is likely in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`. Claude Code v2.1.142 and later ignore `auto` from those files so a repository cannot grant itself auto mode. Move it to `~/.claude/settings.json`.' The VS Code tab independently restates it ('Claude Code ignores `defaultMode: "auto"` in project and local settings'). The guidance's parallel to the claim-25 autoMode scope exclusion is a fair generalization — both are stated by the docs as repo-cannot-escalate-itself protections.

statement: Four CLI subcommands inspect auto mode configuration: `claude auto-mode defaults` prints the built-in environment/allow/soft_deny/hard_deny rules as JSON, `claude auto-mode config` prints the effective configuration with settings applied, `claude auto-mode critique` gives AI feedback on custom rules, and `claude auto-mode reset` (v2.1.212 or later) removes the `autoMode` section from user settings. `claude auto-mode defaults --label <prefix>` (v2.1.208+) prints a single rule by case-insensitive label prefix.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI; `reset` requires v2.1.212+, `--label` requires v2.1.208+
candidate_guidance: `claude auto-mode config` is the verification step after any settings change - it expands `"$defaults"` in place so you can confirm you did not accidentally replace a built-in list. Make it the mandatory follow-up to editing `autoMode`.

sources.title: Configure auto mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: All four subcommands and both version gates verified in the 'Inspect the defaults and your effective config' section. `defaults` prints the built-in four lists as JSON; `config` prints 'what the classifier actually uses as JSON, with your settings applied where set and defaults otherwise'; `critique` gives 'AI feedback on your custom `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` rules'; `reset` 'requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later and removes the `autoMode` section from your user settings file' (with a confirmation prompt and `--yes`, and managed/`--settings` rules surviving). The `--label` flag is documented with 'Matching is a case-insensitive prefix on each rule's label' and 'Requires Claude Code v2.1.208 or later.' The guidance's verification-step recommendation is the docs' own instruction: 'Run `claude auto-mode config` after saving your settings to confirm the effective rules are what you expect, with "$defaults" expanded in place.'

statement: The `PermissionDenied` hook event fires when a tool call is denied by the auto mode classifier. It is not block-capable, and a handler can return `hookSpecificOutput` with `hookEventName: "PermissionDenied"` and `retry: true` to tell the model it may retry the denied tool call.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, `auto` permission mode with PermissionDenied hooks
candidate_guidance: This is the programmatic surface for reacting to classifier denials - useful for telemetry on which rules fire most often in a given repo, which is the evidence you need before adding `autoMode.environment` entries.

reason: Three tier-1 pages agree. The guide's event table: '`PermissionDenied` | When a tool call is denied by the auto mode classifier. Return `{retry: true}` to tell the model it may retry the denied tool call.' The reference's blocking table marks it 'Can block? No' with 'Exit code and stderr are ignored because the denial already occurred. Use JSON `hookSpecificOutput.retry: true` to tell the model it may retry.' auto-mode-config closes the loop on the use case: 'To react to denials programmatically, use the `PermissionDenied` hook.' The `hookEventName` field the claim names inside `hookSpecificOutput` is the documented convention across every event that uses that envelope (PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit and PermissionRequest examples all carry it), so the output shape is consistent with the reference even though the PermissionDenied snippet abbreviates it. statement: Writes to protected paths are never auto-approved in any mode except `bypassPermissions`: they are prompted in `default`, `acceptEdits` and `plan`, routed to the classifier in `auto`, denied in `dontAsk`, and allowed in `bypassPermissions`. `permissions.allow` rules do not pre-approve protected-path writes because the safety check runs before allow-rule evaluation. Protected locations include `.git`, `.claude` (except `.claude/worktrees`), `.vscode`, `.idea`, `.devcontainer`, shell rc files, `.envrc`, `.npmrc`, `.mcp.json` and `.claude.json`.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, all permission modes
candidate_guidance: An entry such as `Edit(.claude/**)` in settings does not change the per-mode outcome - this is a second instance of the general pattern that Claude Code's own configuration surface is protected against self-modification by the agent.

statement: `autoMode.classifyAllShell: true` suspends every Bash and PowerShell allow rule while auto mode is active so the classifier evaluates every shell command regardless of the allow list; the key requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later and earlier versions ignore it.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.193+, `autoMode.classifyAllShell` setting, `auto` permission mode only
candidate_guidance: This is the explicit trade of latency for coverage: every shell command becomes a classifier round-trip and counts as a classifier call against token usage. Worth it where narrow allow rules could smuggle an unanticipated flag or script path past the classifier.

sources.title: Configure auto mode - Claude Code Docs

reason: Verbatim in 'Route all shell commands through the classifier': 'Set `autoMode.classifyAllShell` to `true` to suspend every Bash and PowerShell allow rule while auto mode is active, so the classifier evaluates every shell command regardless of your allow list.' Version gate is an explicit Note: '`autoMode.classifyAllShell` requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later. Earlier versions ignore the key and continue to carry narrow shell allow rules into auto mode.' statement: Claude Code loads only the first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, at the start of every conversation; content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x auto memory (docs verified at v2.1.214)
candidate_guidance: Treat MEMORY.md strictly as a one-line-per-entry index. Any guidance that must be seen every session has to fit inside the first 200 lines / 25KB; push detail into topic files that Claude reads on demand.

statement: Auto memory is stored per project at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ with a MEMORY.md entrypoint plus optional topic files; the <project> path is derived from the git repository, so all worktrees and subdirectories of one repo share a single auto memory directory, and the files are machine-local (not synced across machines or cloud environments).
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x auto memory (docs verified at v2.1.214)
candidate_guidance: Do not expect auto memory to travel between machines or into cloud sessions. Anything that must be portable or team-visible belongs in a committed CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules/ file, not auto memory.

statement: Auto-compaction timing is not uniform across models: Claude Code compacts proactively when CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW is set, in cloud sessions, on Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 without extended context (which compact at the 200K boundary by default), and on Sonnet 5 (where proactive compaction applies at the model's own default threshold, about 967K tokens), whereas in other cases such as a local session on Opus 4.8, auto-compaction triggers only when the conversation reaches the model's context limit.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x, model-dependent (docs verified at v2.1.214)
candidate_guidance: Any claim of the form 'Claude Code compacts at N%' is model- and environment-dependent. Benchmarks comparing context strategies must pin the model and note whether compaction was proactive or at-limit, or the arms are not comparable. Note specifically that Sonnet 5 compacts proactively at its own ~967K default while Opus 4.8 locally does not compact until the context limit, so a Sonnet-vs-Opus comparison silently varies the compaction regime as well as the model.

statement: Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token context window. For Opus and Sonnet 4.6 it is selected via the [1m] suffix on aliases or full model names (for example /model opus[1m] or /model claude-opus-4-8[1m]); Sonnet 5 is the exception, running at 1M natively on the Anthropic API with no [1m] variant to select. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 removes 1M variants from the model picker and treats Sonnet 5 sessions as having a 200K window.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x model configuration (docs verified at v2.1.214)
candidate_guidance: The 1M window uses standard model pricing with no premium for tokens beyond 200K, so the cost argument against extended context is about token volume, not rate. Do not write '[1m]' into any Sonnet 5 configuration: the suffix has no effect there (sonnet[1m] is documented as a no-op when sonnet already resolves to Sonnet 5), and the one place it does matter for Sonnet 5 is behind an LLM gateway, where selecting the 1M picker row maps to sonnet[1m]. On Bedrock, Google Cloud Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry the [1m] suffix is read per environment variable, not per model, and Sonnet 5 never needs it there.

statement: CLAUDE.md supports @path/to/import syntax whose files are expanded and loaded into context at launch, recursively to a maximum depth of four hops; import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks, so a backticked `@README` stays literal.

statement: CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself, so there is no guarantee of strict compliance; for instructions that must run at a fixed lifecycle point Anthropic directs users to hooks, and for system-prompt-level text to --append-system-prompt.

statement: As of Claude Code v2.1.210, after Claude writes to MEMORY.md the file is measured against the 200-line and 25KB read limits: a near-limit file triggers a reminder to shorten it, and an over-limit file still writes successfully but returns an error telling Claude to rewrite the index. The check measures only content that actually loads, since YAML frontmatter and block-level HTML comments are stripped before the index is loaded; the version that introduced this loaded-content-only measurement is contested between two tier-1 Anthropic sources, with /en/memory annotating it as v2.1.211 and the changelog crediting it to v2.1.193 (2026-06-25).
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.210 / v2.1.211 and later
candidate_guidance: Self-maintaining memory index behavior is now enforced by the harness rather than left to the model's judgment, and any version from v2.1.211 onward has both the error and the loaded-content-only measurement. Do not pin automation or documentation to v2.1.211 as the introduction version for the loaded-content-only check: Anthropic's own changelog dates that improvement to v2.1.193, and the two sources are not reconcilable from published text alone. The most likely reconciliation, which is inference rather than documented fact, is that v2.1.193 fixed the older warning path and v2.1.211 fixed the newer error path introduced in v2.1.210. If a version boundary is load-bearing, test it empirically.

statement: Subagents run in a separate context window that loads CLAUDE.md and the same MCP and skill setup but not the main conversation's history or auto memory; the built-in Explore and Plan agents are an exception and skip CLAUDE.md for a smaller context. A fork is a further exception, inheriting the parent conversation and system prompt, and a subagent's own auto memory (enabled with the subagent memory field) is a separate directory.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x subagents (docs verified at v2.1.214)
candidate_guidance: Subagent isolation is the primary structural lever for context economy, but it also means a subagent does not inherit learned context. Anything a custom subagent needs must be in the spawn prompt, CLAUDE.md, or its own memory directory. Do not rely on CLAUDE.md reaching the built-in Explore and Plan agents at all: they skip it, so any constraint those agents must respect belongs in the spawn prompt or in an enforcement layer (hooks, permissions.deny), not in CLAUDE.md.

statement: Anthropic reports that on an internal agentic-search evaluation, combining the memory tool with context editing improved performance by 39% over baseline and context editing alone delivered a 29% improvement, and that in a 100-turn web search evaluation context editing reduced token consumption by 84% while enabling workflows that would otherwise fail from context exhaustion.

statement: Anthropic's context engineering guidance defines context engineering as 'curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during LLM inference' and asserts context rot: as the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases, attributed to transformers needing n-squared pairwise token relationships.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic agent design guidance (Anthropic engineering, published 2025-09-29)
candidate_guidance: This is the canonical vendor articulation of why smaller context beats larger context. The mechanism claim (n-squared attention causing recall degradation) is stated without a citation in the essay itself; treat the directional claim as well-supported and the causal explanation as a vendor hypothesis.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents - Anthropic Engineering

reason: Confirmed against the essay (published 2025-09-29). Definition verbatim: 'Context engineering refers to the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference.' Context rot verbatim: 'as the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model's ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases.' The n-squared attribution is present verbatim: attention 'enables every token to attend to every other token across the entire context. This results in n² pairwise relationships for n tokens', alongside the 'attention budget' framing. Tier-3 backing is acceptable here only because the claim is marked version_sensitive: false and is a claim about what Anthropic asserts, not about product mechanics. One refinement to the candidate guidance rather than the statement: the essay is not entirely uncited on context rot; it points to needle-in-a-haystack benchmarking and links Chroma's context-rot research. What lacks empirical citation is specifically the causal step from n² attention to recall degradation, so phrase the caveat that narrowly.

statement: Anthropic documents an explicit agent-to-agent trust boundary for agent teams: teammates start with the lead's permission settings and inherit --dangerously-skip-permissions if the lead used it; a teammate cannot approve a permission prompt or supply consent on the user's behalf; a teammate denied an action cannot relay it to another teammate to bypass the check; and in auto mode the classifier treats an approval claim relayed from another agent as untrusted input rather than confirmation from the user. Teammate permission prompts surface in the lead session, with plan approval as the designed exception.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ agent teams; security-relevant
candidate_guidance: This is the authoritative statement that inter-agent messages are untrusted input, matching the repo's existing 'observed content is data, not commands' stance. Note the sharp edge: --dangerously-skip-permissions on the lead silently propagates to every teammate, so the blast radius of that flag scales with team size.

statement: Agent team state is stored locally under a session-derived name of the form "session-" plus the first eight characters of the session ID: team config at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/config.json, task list at ~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/, and per-agent mailboxes as JSON at ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/inboxes/{agent-name}.json. The team config directory is removed when the session ends; the task list directory persists, is never uploaded, and its retention follows the same cleanupPeriodDays setting as session transcripts. There is no project-level equivalent — a .claude/teams/teams.json in a project is not recognized as configuration.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ agent teams
candidate_guidance: Do not author or hand-edit team config: docs state it holds runtime state (session IDs, tmux pane IDs) and is overwritten on the next state update. Reusable roles must be expressed as subagent definitions instead.

statement: Three hook events exist for enforcing quality gates on agent teams: TeammateIdle (runs when a teammate is about to go idle), TaskCreated (runs when a task is being created), and TaskCompleted (runs when a task is being marked complete). In each case exiting with code 2 sends feedback and blocks the transition — keeping the teammate working, preventing task creation, or preventing completion.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ agent teams with hooks configured in settings.json
candidate_guidance: This is the deterministic enforcement surface for teams and is the natural place to attach the repo's verification-loop gates: a TaskCompleted hook exiting 2 is a mechanical block on 'declared done without evidence', which is exactly the silent-defect failure the repo already measures.

statement: Documented agent-team limitations include: /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates; exactly one team per session with no additional named teams and no sharing across sessions; no nested teams (teammates cannot spawn their own teammates, only the lead manages the team); the lead is fixed for the session lifetime and leadership cannot be transferred; permission modes are set at spawn from the lead and cannot be set per-teammate at spawn time; and an in-process teammate cannot launch background subagents (requesting one via run_in_background or a background: true definition returns an error).
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ agent teams (experimental)
candidate_guidance: The no-resumption and one-team-per-session limits mean teams are unsuitable for long-running multi-session workstreams like the ones this repo logs; treat a team as a single-session burst and persist findings to the workstream .md before the session ends.

statement: A teammate can be spawned from an existing subagent definition of any scope (project, user, plugin, or CLI-defined). On that path the teammate honors the definition's tools allowlist and model, and the definition's body is appended to the teammate's system prompt as additional instructions rather than replacing it. The skills and mcpServers frontmatter fields are NOT applied when a definition runs as a teammate — teammates load skills and MCP servers from project and user settings like a regular session. Team coordination tools such as SendMessage and the task management tools remain available even when tools restricts other tools.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ agent teams
candidate_guidance: This is the one supported way to define reusable teammate roles. Note the asymmetry as a trap: a subagent definition that relies on skills: or mcpServers: will silently lose those when reused as a teammate, so roles intended for both paths must not depend on them.

statement: As of Claude Code v2.1.198 subagents run in the background by default, with Claude running one in the foreground only when it needs the result before continuing; before v2.1.198 Claude chose per task. The frontmatter field background: true forces background execution always. Setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 disables all background task functionality and takes precedence over fork mode; setting CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=1 makes every subagent run in the background and nullifies the background frontmatter field because fork mode removes the run_in_background parameter from the Agent tool.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.198+ for the default change; env vars vendor-specific
candidate_guidance: The changed default alters observed timing and interleaving of subagent results, which matters for any repo harness that assumed synchronous subagent returns. As of v2.1.211 Claude waits for the completion notification before reporting a background subagent's results.

statement: The subagent frontmatter field isolation: worktree runs the subagent in a temporary git worktree, giving it an isolated copy of the repository branched by default from the repository's default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD, with the worktree automatically cleaned up if the subagent makes no changes. Claude Code v2.1.210 fixed isolation: 'worktree' subagents being able to run git-mutating commands against the main repo checkout.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x; v2.1.210+ for the containment fix
candidate_guidance: This is the concrete mechanism that makes parallel *implementation* safe, and it directly answers the docs' own 'two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites' warning — but it exists for subagents, not for agent-team teammates. Note the base-branch subtlety: worktrees branch from the default branch, not from your current HEAD, so uncommitted or branch-local work is not visible to the subagent.

statement: Subagent name collisions resolve by scope priority, with project .claude/agents/ (priority 3) outranking user ~/.claude/agents/ (priority 4), and managed subagents deployed by administrators in the managed settings directory taking precedence over both project and user subagents of the same name. Project subagents are discovered by walking up from the current working directory so every .claude/agents/ between there and the repo root is scanned, and as of v2.1.178 the definition closest to the working directory wins on collision. Both .claude/agents/ and ~/.claude/agents/ are scanned recursively; subdirectory paths do not affect identity, which comes only from the name frontmatter field.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.178+ for nearest-wins nested resolution
candidate_guidance: Relevant to this repo's multi-repo GithubRepos layout: nested .claude/agents/ directories per repo will shadow user-level definitions of the same name, so name collisions across repos are silent overrides rather than errors.

As of v2.1.178, when more than one of these nested directories defines the same name, Claude Code uses the definition closest to the working directory.' Recursive scanning and name-only identity also verbatim. This pass additionally resolves the researcher's open question: the full ordering is 1 = managed settings, 2 = --agents CLI flag, 3 = project, 4 = user, 5 = plugin (lowest). One caveat for the repo's multi-repo layout: within a single directory (including its subfolders) duplicate names resolve by filesystem read order, not documented precedence.

statement: Cognition's "Don't Build Multi-Agents" argues against multi-agent architectures on two stated principles — "Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages" and "Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results" — and recommends single-threaded linear agents as the default, with a specialized history-compression model for long tasks (noted as hard to get right). The named failure modes are miscommunication of subtasks, conflicting assumptions between parallel subagents with no visibility into each other's decisions, and dispersed decision-making, illustrated by a Flappy Bird example where subagents produced mutually incompatible components.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic architectural argument; published mid-2025, predates Claude Code agent teams
candidate_guidance: The strongest available statement of the null-hypothesis position and a good match for this repo's measured nulls on scaffolding. Its force is conceptual, not empirical — no benchmark accompanies it. Note the interesting tension: Anthropic's agent-teams design partially answers principle 1 via shared task lists and direct messaging, but principle 2 remains unanswered for same-file parallel edits, which is exactly where Anthropic's own docs also warn off.

statement: A Google Research study evaluated 180 agent configurations across 5 canonical architectures (single-agent, independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid), 4 benchmarks (Finance-Agent, BrowseComp-Plus, PlanCraft, Workbench), and 3 model families (OpenAI GPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude), and reports that independent multi-agent systems amplified errors 17.2x relative to the single-agent baseline while centralized orchestration held amplification to 4.4x, with the orchestrator acting as a validation bottleneck.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; published 2026-01-28; note that none of the four benchmarks is a software-engineering benchmark
candidate_guidance: The best-sourced quantitative evidence found for the helps-vs-harms question, and it argues specifically against *leaderless* fan-out rather than against multi-agent per se. Carry the caveat prominently: the benchmark suite contains no coding task, so transfer to Claude Code coding work is unestablished and this should not be promoted as a coding claim without a held-out coding replication.

The figures are verbatim: 'Independent multi-agent systems (agents working in parallel without talking) amplified errors by 17.2x... Centralized systems (with an orchestrator) contained this amplification to just 4.4x', with the orchestrator described as a validation bottleneck that catches errors before they propagate, relative to a single-agent baseline. Published January 28, 2026. The claim's standing caveat is factually correct and load-bearing: none of the four benchmarks is a software-engineering benchmark, so the coding transfer is genuinely unestablished and should not be promoted as a coding claim.

statement: The same Google Research study reports a task-shape dependence: on the parallelizable Finance-Agent benchmark, centralized multi-agent coordination improved results by +80.9%, while on the sequential PlanCraft benchmark all multi-agent variants degraded performance by 39-70% relative to a single agent.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; non-coding benchmarks; published 2026-01-28
candidate_guidance: This is independent quantitative corroboration of Anthropic's own qualitative rule that teams help on parallelizable work and hurt on sequential work. The magnitude of the sequential penalty (39-70%) is the sharpest argument available for gating multi-agent use on a decomposability check rather than defaulting to it.

sources.title: Towards a science of scaling agent systems: When and why agent systems work - Google Research

reason: Both figures verified: 'On parallelizable tasks like financial reasoning... centralized coordination improved performance by 80.9% over a single agent' and 'On tasks requiring strict sequential reasoning (like planning in PlanCraft), every multi-agent variant we tested degraded performance by 39-70%.' The claim's attribution of the gain specifically to centralized coordination (not multi-agent generally) is faithful to the source and matters — the same study shows independent fan-out amplifying errors. This is genuine independent corroboration of the Anthropic qualitative rule in claim 05, from a different vendor and a different task suite, so the repo can legitimately state it as a cross-source regularity while keeping the non-coding-benchmark caveat attached.

statement: The Google Research study fits a predictive model (R^2 = 0.513) that selects the optimal coordination architecture from measurable task properties — tool count, decomposability, sequential dependencies, and tool density — and reports it correctly identifies the optimal coordination strategy for 87% of unseen task configurations.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; published 2026-01-28; R^2 = 0.513 indicates roughly half of variance unexplained

Treat the 87% figure as architecture-selection accuracy, not task success rate.

statement: A Codex hook signals a decision by exiting with code 2 and writing a reason to stderr. This path is documented for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStop, and Stop, but the meaning of the stderr text differs by event: it is a blocking reason for PreToolUse and UserPromptSubmit, a feedback reason for PostToolUse (the tool has already executed, so nothing is prevented), and a continuation reason for SubagentStop and Stop. Exit 0 with no output is treated as success and Codex continues. PermissionRequest is not among the events documented for the exit-2 path.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20
candidate_guidance: Exit 2 plus stderr is the low-ceremony signaling path; structured JSON on stdout is the richer alternative. Do not assume exit 2 blocks on every event that accepts it -- only PreToolUse and UserPromptSubmit prevent the action outright. On PostToolUse the tool call has already run, so exit 2 delivers feedback rather than prevention; a PostToolUse handler written as a policy blocker will not stop anything and gives false assurance. On SubagentStop and Stop the stderr text is a continuation reason. Note exit 0 with no output means success and continue, so a handler that crashes to exit 0 fails open -- write hooks to fail closed explicitly.

sources.title: Codex Hooks

reason: The event list and the exit-2-plus-stderr mechanism are correct and directly supported, including Stop, which I confirmed against the page's grouped sentence for SubagentStop and Stop. But the claim flattens three distinct documented semantics into "the blocking reason". The page uses "blocking reason" for PreToolUse and UserPromptSubmit, "feedback reason" for PostToolUse, and "continuation reason" for SubagentStop and Stop. This is load-bearing, not pedantic: PostToolUse fires after execution, so an operator who reads the original wording could build a PostToolUse policy blocker that silently prevents nothing -- precisely the false-coverage failure this bucket is trying to guard against. Corrected rather than confirmed so the distinction survives into the contract. Also verified exit 0 with no output is "treated as success and Codex continues", supporting the fail-open warning already in the guidance.

statement: Codex records hook trust against the hook's current hash: "Codex records trust against the hook's current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted."

candidate_guidance: This is the core of the Codex hook trust model and has a direct operational consequence: editing a trusted hook silently disables it until re-reviewed. Any repo that ships hooks must document that teammates will see hooks skipped after a pull until they re-trust them. Contrast with the fail-open risk in claim 06.

sources.title: Codex Hooks

reason: Quoted sentence matches the page verbatim: "Codex records trust against the hook's current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted." The guidance's operational consequence -- that editing a trusted hook disables it until re-reviewed, and that teammates see hooks skipped after a pull -- follows directly from hash-based trust. Note the open question about hash scope (command string only vs full definition including matcher and timeout) remains genuinely unresolved on this page and should stay in open_questions.

statement: The CLI flag --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust runs enabled hooks without requiring persisted hook trust for that invocation.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20 (latest stable 0.144.6)
candidate_guidance: Exact flag spelling verified against the official page. Scope is per-invocation, not persistent. Treat as CI-only; using it interactively defeats the hash-based review gate in claim 07. Do not bake into shared developer scripts.

The docs' own framing ("one-off automation that already vets hook sources outside Codex") supports the guidance's CI-only recommendation.

statement: Hooks originating from system, MDM, cloud, or requirements.toml sources are marked as managed, are trusted by policy, and cannot be disabled from the user hook browser.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20
candidate_guidance: This is the enterprise enforcement path: managed hooks skip the per-user review gate and are not user-disableable, which is what makes them viable for audit and policy controls. Conversely it means an admin-pushed hook runs without individual consent, so it is a meaningful trust delegation worth stating explicitly in any org policy doc.

statement: The config key project_doc_max_bytes controls the byte limit applied when building project instructions from AGENTS.md, and defaults to 32 KiB.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20

Caveat: the two official pages describe the limit's unit of application differently -- config-advanced calls it max bytes read per AGENTS.md file, while the AGENTS.md page describes it as the combined accumulated size. See open_questions before writing guidance that depends on which reading is correct.
