reason: The claim as stated is supported and the caveat it carries is accurate. The AGENTS.md page gives the 32 KiB default; the Configuration Reference describes the key as "Maximum bytes read from AGENTS.md when building project instructions" and states no default, exactly as the claim says. I independently reproduced the documented conflict rather than taking it on trust: config-advanced describes the value as how much to read from each AGENTS.md file (per-file), while the AGENTS.md page says Codex "stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit" (accumulated). These imply materially different truncation behavior in a monorepo. The researcher was right to emit the claim while routing the semantics to open_questions rather than shipping sizing guidance; keep it there until resolved empirically against 0.144.6.

statement: Codex AGENTS.md discovery starts at global scope (~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md if present, otherwise ~/.codex/AGENTS.md), then walks from the project root -- typically the Git root -- down to the current working directory, checking each level for AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then configured fallback names.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20
candidate_guidance: Note the direction: root downward to cwd, not cwd upward. The AGENTS.override.md filename is officially documented ("Use ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md when you need a temporary global override without deleting the base file") and is a genuinely useful pattern for temporarily suspending global instructions without deleting them.

sources.title: Codex AGENTS.md

reason: Every element verified. Global scope prefers ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md and falls back to ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, with the page noting Codex uses only the first non-empty file at that level. Project traversal is stated as "Starting at the project root (typically the Git root), Codex walks down to your current working directory" -- confirming the root-downward direction the guidance flags, which is the counterintuitive part and worth the emphasis. Per-level precedence is "AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then any fallback names". The override sentence is verbatim: "Use ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md when you need a temporary global override without deleting the base file."

statement: Codex concatenates discovered AGENTS.md files from root downward separated by blank lines, and files closer to the current directory override earlier guidance because they appear later in the combined prompt.
applicability: Codex CLI, docs current as of 2026-07-20
candidate_guidance: The override mechanism is positional, not structural -- there is no merge or key-level resolution, just later-text-wins ordering. Practical consequence for monorepos: a nested AGENTS.md should restate the specific rule it intends to override, because a general parent rule remains in the prompt and is only outranked by proximity.

statement: An open issue on the official openai/codex repository (#20204, opened 2026-04-29) reports that PreToolUse hook events are emitted by only four tool categories -- shell/Bash, unified_exec, apply_patch, and mcp -- while other tool handlers fall back to a trait default of None and never fire hooks, leaving gaps including filesystem reads (list_dir, view_image).
applicability: Codex CLI; report filed against a pre-0.144 build, current status against 0.144.6 unconfirmed
candidate_guidance: LOW CONFIDENCE and deliberately scoped: this is an unresolved community bug report on the official repo, NOT documented behavior, and no maintainer confirmation or fix version was found. Do not state it as fact. It is however a high-value hypothesis to test before relying on PreToolUse as a complete audit boundary -- if true, a hook-based policy that assumes it sees every tool call would miss file reads entirely. Recommend empirical verification against the pinned version before any guidance is promoted.

sources.title: openai/codex issue #20204: Inconsistent PreToolUse hook coverage across tool handlers (most tools never emit hook events)

reason: Confirmed strictly as worded -- the claim asserts that an open issue reports a behavior, and that meta-statement is precisely true. Verified on the issue page: title "Inconsistent PreToolUse hook coverage across tool handlers (most tools never emit hook events)", state open, opened 2026-04-29, and the body states only shell (Bash), unified_exec, apply_patch, and mcp opt in while every other handler in core/src/tools/handlers/ falls back to the trait default (None), explicitly naming list_dir and view_image as filesystem reads that emit nothing. No maintainer response, no linked PR, no fix version. Confidence is medium rather than high because the operationally decisive fact -- whether this still reproduces on 0.144.6 -- is unverified, and a report filed against a pre-0.144 build may well be stale. Do not let this confirmation launder an unproven bug into documented behavior: it verifies the report exists and says what the researcher claims, nothing about current runtime truth. The low-confidence framing and the empirical-verification-before-promotion condition in the candidate guidance must both be preserved verbatim. This remains the highest-value empirical test in the bucket, since if it holds, PreToolUse is not a complete audit boundary and any hook-based policy assuming total tool coverage has a hole around file reads.

statement: Under bubblewrap the Codex Linux sandbox mounts the filesystem read-only by default via `--ro-bind / /`, grants writable roots via `--bind <root> <root>`, and re-applies `.git` and `.codex` subpaths as read-only via `--ro-bind`.
applicability: Codex CLI 0.144.x on Linux
candidate_guidance: Cite this as the concrete enforcement behind 'workspace-write': the agent cannot rewrite git history or its own Codex config inside a writable root without an approval escalation.

statement: The Codex Linux sandbox applies `--unshare-user` and `--unshare-pid`, and additionally applies `--unshare-net` when network is restricted AND no proxy routing is in use, plus `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` and an in-process seccomp network filter.
applicability: Codex CLI 0.144.x on Linux
candidate_guidance: Use as the technical basis for network-off-by-default on Linux, but state the condition precisely: the network namespace is NOT unshared when traffic is routed through the Codex network proxy. In that configuration egress control rests on the `features.network_proxy` domain allowlist rather than on namespace isolation — which matters because the allowlist is explicitly best-effort (see claim 17). `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` blocks setuid escalation inside the sandbox and remains the sharpest property to cite in any published threat model.

statement: Codex `sandbox_mode` accepts exactly three values: `read-only`, `workspace-write`, and `danger-full-access`. Under `workspace-write` the agent runs with network access turned off by default and write permissions limited to the active workspace (the current directory plus temporary directories like /tmp). The documentation does NOT declare a single global default: on launch Codex detects whether the folder is version-controlled and recommends the `Auto` preset (`--sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval on-request`) for version-controlled folders and `Read Only` for folders that are not.
applicability: Codex CLI 0.144.x
candidate_guidance: Set `sandbox_mode` explicitly in repo config rather than relying on an implied default, because the effective starting mode is context-dependent on whether the folder is version-controlled. `workspace-write` is the right explicit repo default and `danger-full-access` should require a recorded justification. These are the canonical spellings: hyphenated, not underscored.

statement: Codex network access when enabled is governed by the `features.network_proxy` `domains` policy, which is unset by default — meaning no external destinations are allowed until `allow` rules are added. Deny rules always win over allow; exact hosts match only themselves; `*.example.com` matches subdomains ONLY; `**.example.com` matches the apex plus subdomains; and a global `*` broadly opens public outbound access. Local/private destinations are blocked by default (`allow_local_binding` defaults to false, and grants broader local/private-network access when set), though an exact local IP literal or a `localhost` allow rule can also permit specific local targets.
applicability: Codex CLI 0.144.x
candidate_guidance: Recommend an explicit domain allowlist rather than `danger-full-access` when an agent needs network, and prefer scoped rules over `*`. Critical detail for any repo template: `*.example.com` covers subdomains ONLY and does NOT match the bare apex domain — use `**.example.com` when both are needed, or a template pinning only `*.` will silently fail on the apex. Also note that `allow_local_binding` is not the only path to local access: an exact local IP literal or `localhost` allow rule grants specific local targets independently. Retain the documented caveat that DNS and IP classification are best-effort, so the allowlist is not a hard exfiltration boundary.

statement: Claude Code's sandboxed Bash tool enforces isolation using OS primitives: Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2. Native Windows and WSL1 are not supported; on Linux/WSL2 the sandbox additionally requires the `socat` package for proxied network traffic, and an optional seccomp filter (installed via `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`) is what blocks Unix domain sockets.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, macOS/Linux/WSL2 only
candidate_guidance: On this Windows 11 machine, the built-in Bash sandbox cannot run natively — it requires running Claude Code inside a WSL2 distribution. Any repo guidance that assumes sandboxed Bash is active must state this platform caveat explicitly, or agents on Windows will silently fall back to unsandboxed execution (see claim 05 on failIfUnavailable).

reason: Every element verified verbatim against the tier-1 primary, fetched 2026-07-20. Docs: 'macOS: uses Seatbelt for sandbox enforcement / Linux: uses bubblewrap for isolation / WSL2: uses bubblewrap, same as Linux' and 'WSL1 is not supported because bubblewrap requires kernel features only available in WSL2' plus 'supports macOS, Linux, and WSL2. WSL1 and native Windows are not supported.' socat is confirmed as one of the two required Linux/WSL2 packages, described as 'the relay used to route network traffic through the sandbox proxy'. The seccomp filter is confirmed optional, 'adds Unix domain socket blocking', installed via 'npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime', and the troubleshooting section states 'the seccomp filter is required to block Unix domain sockets'. The Windows guidance is directly supported: 'On Windows, run Claude Code inside a WSL2 distribution' and 'The sandbox does not run on native Windows, so if your fleet includes Windows hosts, scope this configuration to macOS and Linux or have those users run Claude Code inside WSL2 or a container.' Separately noted for the estate: a WSL2 caveat the claim omits but which matters here — sandboxed commands cannot launch Windows binaries (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, anything under /mnt/c/), because WSL hands these to the Windows host over a Unix socket that the sandbox blocks; such commands must go in excludedCommands.

statement: By default the Claude Code Bash sandbox grants read access to the entire computer except certain denied directories. The official documentation states this default still allows reading credential files such as `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.ssh/`. Write access defaults to the current working directory plus the session temp directory only.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, sandbox enabled with default filesystem settings
candidate_guidance: Enabling the sandbox does NOT protect secrets from being read. This is the single most likely false-sense-of-security in the repo's guidance: 'sandbox on' constrains writes and egress, not reads. Any recommendation to enable sandboxing should be paired with an explicit `sandbox.credentials` or `denyRead` block (claim 03), otherwise the read side of the lethal trifecta remains wide open.

reason: Confirmed near-verbatim against the tier-1 primary. Docs, 'Default read behavior': 'read access to the entire computer, except certain denied directories. Note that this default still allows reading credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh/.' The 'Default write behavior' bullet reads 'read and write access to the current working directory and its subdirectories, plus the session temp directory that $TMPDIR points to', and the Get Started section uses the same 'only' framing the claim adopts: 'commands inside the sandbox can write only to the working directory and the session temp directory'. Two documented refinements worth carrying but not sufficient to downgrade the verdict: (a) write access includes subdirectories of the cwd; (b) one narrow default exception to 'only' exists — in a linked git worktree the sandbox also permits writes to the main repository's shared .git directory so git commit can update refs and the index, though writes to hooks/ and config inside it remain denied. The guidance's core point is exactly right and is reinforced by the docs' own org-configuration section, which advises adding sandbox.credentials entries for ~/.aws and ~/.ssh 'since the default read policy still allows them'.

statement: The `sandbox.credentials` settings block declares credential files and environment variables to protect from sandboxed commands and requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later. File entries support only `"mode": "deny"`. Environment-variable entries additionally support `"mode": "mask"`, which requires Claude Code v2.1.199 or later and requires `sandbox.network.tlsTerminate` to be set, because the proxy must terminate TLS to substitute the real credential for the per-session sentinel value.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.187+ for `deny`; v2.1.199+ for `mask`
candidate_guidance: Recommend a concrete `sandbox.credentials` starter block in repo guidance (deny `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.ssh`; deny or mask `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`NPM_TOKEN`). Note that `mask` fails closed — without `network.tlsTerminate` the sentinel reaches the server and auth fails, which Claude Code reports at startup. Also note `mask` entries are ignored from a repository's `.claude/settings.json` (claim 06), so they must live in user or managed settings.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool - Claude Code Docs

reason: All four version/behaviour assertions verified verbatim. 'The sandbox.credentials setting declares credential files and environment variables to protect from sandboxed commands... Requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later.' 'File entries support only "mode": "deny". Environment variable entries also accept "mode": "mask".' 'Requires Claude Code v2.1.199 or later.' The TLS rationale is stated exactly as the claim renders it: 'The proxy substitutes the credential inside request contents, so it has to see them. Set network.tlsTerminate so the proxy terminates TLS itself. Without it, masking fails closed: the command still sees only the sentinel, but the sentinel reaches the server unchanged and authentication fails. Claude Code reports this misconfiguration at startup.' The guidance's scope caveat is also confirmed: 'mask entries, network.tlsTerminate, and credentials.allowPlaintextInject in a repository's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json are ignored' — honored only from user settings, managed settings, and the --settings CLI flag. Two additions worth folding into the starter block: deny entries merge across all scopes and can only narrow access (no scope can remove another scope's deny), and where a variable is listed both deny and mask, deny wins. Also note each injectHosts entry must itself be covered by network.allowedDomains, and there is no built-in credential deny list — only what you enumerate is protected.

statement: Claude Code's built-in sandbox proxy enforces its domain allowlist based on the client-supplied hostname and by default does not terminate or inspect TLS. The documentation warns that code running inside the sandbox can potentially use domain fronting or similar techniques to reach hosts outside the allowlist, and that allowing broad domains such as `github.com` can create paths for data exfiltration.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, built-in sandbox proxy with default (non-TLS-terminating) configuration
candidate_guidance: Treat the sandbox egress allowlist as a blast-radius reducer, not an exfiltration boundary. Repo guidance should keep `allowedDomains` narrow and specific (avoid bare `github.com` / wildcard entries), and state that stronger guarantees require a custom TLS-terminating proxy with its CA installed inside the sandbox. The docs call stronger TLS-aware network isolation an active area of development, so recheck this each cycle.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool - Claude Code Docs

reason: Confirmed verbatim from the Security limitations section. 'The built-in proxy enforces the allowlist based on the requested hostname and, by default, does not terminate or inspect TLS traffic.' The warning reads: 'Allowing broad domains such as github.com can create paths for data exfiltration. Because the proxy makes its allow decision from the client-supplied hostname without inspecting TLS, code running inside the sandbox can potentially use domain fronting or similar techniques to reach hosts outside the allowlist. If your threat model requires stronger guarantees, configure a custom proxy that terminates TLS and inspects traffic, and install its CA certificate inside the sandbox. Stronger TLS-aware network isolation is an active area of development.' The guidance's recheck advice is well founded — that last sentence is an explicit vendor signal of in-flight change. The docs independently support the guidance's caution about tlsTerminate not being a fix: it 'terminates TLS at the proxy for mask credential substitution but does not add content filtering.' Also relevant to keeping allowlists narrow: deniedDomains blocks specific domains even when a broader allowedDomains wildcard would otherwise permit them, and the docs frame the whole section with 'Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary.'

statement: By default, if the Claude Code sandbox cannot start because dependencies are missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code shows a warning and runs commands WITHOUT sandboxing. Setting `sandbox.failIfUnavailable` to `true` makes this a hard failure instead.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, all supported platforms
candidate_guidance: This is a fail-open default. Any repo policy that claims 'agents run sandboxed' is unenforced unless `failIfUnavailable: true` is set in managed settings. Recommend it for any unattended or CI-driven agent run; without it, a missing bubblewrap package silently downgrades the security posture with only a warning.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool - Claude Code Docs

reason: Confirmed verbatim. The docs carry this as a Warning: 'By default, if the sandbox cannot start because dependencies are missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code shows a warning and runs commands without sandboxing. To make this a hard failure instead, set sandbox.failIfUnavailable to true. This is intended for managed deployments that require sandboxing as a security gate.' The managed-settings section restates the mechanism concretely: 'failIfUnavailable: a missing dependency such as bubblewrap on Linux blocks Claude Code from starting rather than showing a warning and falling back to unsandboxed execution.' The guidance's fail-open characterisation and its CI/unattended recommendation both track the vendor's own stated intent. This claim compounds directly with claim 01 for this estate: on native Windows the platform is unsupported, so the default path is precisely the silent downgrade described.

statement: In Claude Code managed settings, boolean sandbox keys such as `enabled` and `failIfUnavailable` override anything a developer sets locally, but array keys such as `excludedCommands` and `allowRead` are merged across every settings scope. `allowManagedReadPathsOnly: true` and `allowManagedDomainsOnly` restrict read paths and network domains to managed values respectively, but `excludedCommands` has no equivalent managed-only lockdown, so a developer can always append entries that run additional commands outside the sandbox.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI with managed settings (MDM file or server-managed settings)
candidate_guidance: Document `excludedCommands` as a permanent, unclosable widening path in any org-level agent policy — the correct mitigation is to keep the managed list narrow and audit local settings, not to assume managed settings are authoritative. Pair with `allowManagedReadPathsOnly` and `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, which DO lock down. This asymmetry between boolean-override and array-merge semantics is a repo-worthy gotcha.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool - Claude Code Docs

reason: Confirmed verbatim from 'Keep developers from widening the policy'. 'For boolean keys such as enabled and failIfUnavailable, Claude Code uses the managed value and ignores anything a developer sets locally. For array keys such as excludedCommands and allowRead, Claude Code merges entries from every scope, so a developer can append entries that widen the policy.' On the lockdowns: 'Set allowManagedReadPathsOnly to true in managed settings so that only allowRead entries from managed settings are honored. User, project, and local allowRead entries are ignored... To lock network domains to the managed values the same way, set allowManagedDomainsOnly.' And the gap is stated by the vendor in the claim's own terms: 'excludedCommands has no equivalent managed-only lockdown, so a developer can always append entries that run additional commands outside the sandbox. Keep the managed list narrow.' The docs elsewhere confirm the general merge rule for filesystem arrays ('paths from every scope are combined, not replaced'), and the network section adds that under allowManagedDomainsOnly non-allowed domains are blocked automatically instead of prompting, and only managed-scope allowedDomains and WebFetch(domain:...) rules are honored. Guidance is sound as written.

statement: Claude Code exposes a `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` Bash parameter as an escape hatch: when a command fails because of sandbox restrictions, Claude analyzes the failure and may retry the command outside the sandbox, where it goes through the regular permission flow. Setting `"allowUnsandboxedCommands": false` (shown as Strict sandbox mode in the `/sandbox` Overrides tab) causes the parameter to be completely ignored.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, sandbox enabled
candidate_guidance: The model itself can elect to leave the sandbox. For blast-radius-sensitive work, recommend `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` in managed settings; where the escape hatch is kept, add an ask rule for `Bash(dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true)` so unsandboxed retries always prompt even under auto mode. Guidance that treats the sandbox boundary as model-independent is wrong unless strict mode is on.

sources.title: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool - Claude Code Docs

reason: Confirmed verbatim, including the UI label. 'when a command fails because of sandbox restrictions, Claude analyzes the failure and may retry the command with the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter. The retried command runs outside the sandbox, so it goes through the regular permission flow: in default mode you get a confirmation prompt; in auto mode the classifier evaluates the underlying command instead of prompting you.' And: 'You can disable this escape hatch by setting "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false in your sandbox settings. When disabled, which the /sandbox Overrides tab shows as Strict sandbox mode, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter is completely ignored and all commands must run sandboxed or be explicitly listed in excludedCommands.' The guidance's specific mitigation is lifted from the docs' own recommendation: 'To be prompted on every unsandboxed retry even in auto mode, add an ask rule for Bash(dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true).' One reinforcing detail for the guidance: even in strict mode the excludedCommands array remains a developer-appendable widening path (claim 06), so strict mode and a narrow managed excludedCommands list must be adopted together to actually make the boundary model-independent.

statement: The Claude Code sandbox automatically denies write access to Claude Code's `settings.json` files at every scope and to the managed settings directory, so a sandboxed command cannot modify its own policy. In v2.1.210 and later, these deny rules resolve symlinks: when a symlink appears at a protected settings file path after startup, the sandbox adds its target to the deny list for the next command.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI; symlink resolution requires v2.1.210+
candidate_guidance: Self-policy-modification is blocked by default, which is the correct design and worth citing in repo guidance as the model for other agent harnesses. Note the symlink-resolution hardening landed only in v2.1.210 — deployments pinned below that version have a linked-settings-file bypass. This corroborates the NVIDIA AI Red Team control on blocking config-file writes (claim 12).

In v2.1.210 and later, the deny rules resolve symlinks: when a symlink appears at a protected settings file path after startup, the sandbox adds its target to the deny list for the next command, so a linked settings file can't be edited through the link.' The v2.1.210 min-version marker is present in the docs source exactly as the claim states, so the guidance's warning about deployments pinned below that version is well grounded. The cross-reference to NVIDIA control (3) in claim 12 is legitimate and holds up — I verified that control independently. One scope caveat to keep attached: this protects settings.json specifically, and NVIDIA's control is broader (all agent configuration files and extensions, including hooks, skills and local MCP configs), so citing this as satisfying NVIDIA control (3) in full would overstate it.

statement: The Claude Code sandbox isolates Bash subprocesses only. The built-in Read, Edit and Write file tools use the permission system directly rather than running through the sandbox, and sandboxed Bash commands inherit the parent process environment by default including any credentials set there. Subagents run in the same process as the parent session and use the same sandbox configuration.
applicability: Claude Code v2.1.x CLI, sandbox enabled
candidate_guidance: Scope statement worth pinning verbatim in the repo: the sandbox is a Bash boundary, not an agent boundary. Read/Edit/Write bypass it entirely and are governed only by permission rules, so `denyRead` on a secrets path does not by itself stop the Read tool. Use `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB` to strip Anthropic and cloud provider credentials from all subprocesses regardless of sandboxing.

reason: Confirmed verbatim from the Scope section. 'The sandbox isolates Bash subprocesses.' 'Built-in file tools: Read, Edit, and Write use the permission system directly rather than running through the sandbox.' 'Environment variables: sandboxed Bash commands inherit the parent process environment by default, including any credentials set there.' 'Subagents: subagents run in the same process as the parent session and use the same sandbox configuration. Bash commands inside a subagent are sandboxed when sandboxing is enabled in the parent session.' The CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB recommendation is the docs' own: it strips 'Anthropic and cloud provider credentials from all subprocesses regardless of sandboxing'. The guidance's inference that denyRead does not stop the Read tool is correct and independently supported by the permissions comparison table, which assigns path blocking for the Read tool to 'Read and Edit deny rules' while sandbox.filesystem.denyRead governs 'subprocess access'. Worth pinning verbatim as the guidance suggests; this is the single most load-bearing scope statement in the bucket.

statement: Meta's "Agents Rule of Two", published 2025-10-31, states that an agent must satisfy no more than two of the following three properties within a session: [A] processing untrustworthy inputs, [B] access to sensitive systems or private data, [C] ability to change state or communicate externally. If an agent requires all three without starting a fresh context window, the agent should not operate autonomously and at minimum requires supervision via human-in-the-loop approval or another reliable means of validation.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic agent architecture guidance; inspired by Chromium security policy and Simon Willison's lethal trifecta framing
candidate_guidance: This is the crispest actionable form of the lethal-trifecta framing and is a better citation than any secondary playbook because it names the escape valve explicitly: a fresh context window resets the session budget. Meta itself states satisfying the Rule of Two is not a finish line and designs that satisfy it can still fail. Use as a design checklist, not a compliance gate.

sources.title: Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security - Meta AI

reason: Confirmed against the tier-1 vendor primary, published 2025-10-31. Meta's formulation: an agent 'must satisfy no more than two of the following three properties within a session to avoid the highest impact consequences of prompt injection' — [A] process untrustworthy inputs, [B] access to sensitive systems or private data, [C] change state or communicate externally. The escape-valve wording the guidance leans on is verbatim: 'If an agent requires all three without starting a new session (i.e., with a fresh context window), then the agent should not be permitted to operate autonomously and at a minimum requires supervision - via human-in-the-loop approval or another reliable means of validation.' The 'not a finish line' caveat is also directly supported: 'satisfying the Agents Rule of Two should not be viewed as sufficient for protecting against other threat vectors', and it is 'a supplement - and not a substitute - for common security principles.' Chromium and Simon Willison's lethal trifecta are both named as inspirations. Independently corroborated: the OWASP v2.01 report I extracted describes the same lethal-trifecta framing and the same practitioner shift 'from trying to prevent injection to constraining what an injected agent can actually accomplish', which is the containment stance this bucket is built on.

statement: OWASP GenAI Security Project published "State of Agentic AI Security and Governance" version 2.01 in June 2026, updating the July 2025 v1.0. The edition ranks prompt injection the leading vulnerability and maps it to six of the ten categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, replacing the prior edition's catalog of plausible threats with disclosed CVEs, vendor advisories and breach reports.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; OWASP State of Agentic AI Security and Governance v2.01 (June 2026)
candidate_guidance: Cite the OWASP primary at genai.owasp.org rather than the Help Net Security summary. The load-bearing structural claim for repo guidance is OWASP's framing that LLMs treat system prompt, user request, and retrieved external text as a single token stream with no reliable way to distinguish commands from data — which is why the repo should frame injection defense as containment (claims 04-07, 12) rather than detection (claims 13-14).

reason: Upgraded from the researcher's position: rather than resting on the tier-5 Help Net Security summary, I downloaded and text-extracted the OWASP primary PDF and verified every element in the document itself. Cover reads 'State of Agentic AI Security and Governance / Version 2.01 / June 2026'. Executive Summary confirms the supersession and the evidentiary shift: 'v1.0 of this report (July 2025) framed agentic risks as a portfolio of plausible threats' and 'What was a list of architectural concerns in 2025 now has production incidents, vendor advisories, and CVEs attached to almost every entry', curated in a Real-World Incidents and Exploits Tracker. The ranking and mapping are stated together: 'Prompt injection (LLM01:2025) is the most prevalent attack technique targeting AI systems... This is why it maps to six of the ten ASI categories' (ASI01-ASI10 being the Top 10 for Agentic Applications IDs, so the claim's rendering is correct). The structural framing the guidance calls load-bearing is verified nearly verbatim: 'LLMs collapse the data plane and the control plane into a single channel: system prompts, user requests, and content retrieved from external sources are all processed as a unified token sequence, with no reliable mechanism to enforce a privilege boundary between them.' One wording precision for the contract: OWASP says 'most prevalent attack technique', not 'leading vulnerability' — substantively equivalent for the guidance, but quote OWASP's phrasing if the line is reproduced. The guidance's instruction to cite the OWASP primary over the trade-press secondary is correct and now actionable, since the six-of-ten detail exists only in the primary.

statement: The NVIDIA AI Red Team names three mandatory controls for sandboxing agentic workflows against indirect prompt injection: (1) network egress controls via tightly scoped allowlists plus DNS resolution limited to trusted resolvers, (2) blocking write operations to files outside the workspace, enforced at OS level via denylists that cannot be overridden by user approval, and (3) blocking writes to configuration files to prevent exploitation of hooks, skills, and local MCP configurations that often run outside a sandbox context.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic agentic workflow deployment; NVIDIA Technical Blog, published 2026-01-30, author Rich Harang
candidate_guidance: These three map almost exactly onto Claude Code sandbox settings (`allowedDomains`, default cwd-only write, protected settings.json) — a useful cross-vendor convergence to cite. The distinctive addition beyond the Claude Code defaults is control (3)'s scope: hooks, skills and local MCP configs are the persistence surface, and NVIDIA's position is that NO user approval should permit agent modification of them. Worth adopting as a hard deny in repo guidance.

sources.title: Practical Security Guidance for Sandboxing Agentic Workflows and Managing Execution Risk | NVIDIA Technical Blog

reason: Confirmed, including the count. I re-fetched specifically to test the 'three mandatory controls' framing and the article does label exactly three as mandatory, headed: (1) 'Network egress except to known-good locations', (2) 'Block file writes outside of the active workspace', (3) 'Block all writes to any agent configuration file or extension'. Everything else in the post is a separate Recommended tier. Control 1 specifies 'tightly scoped allowlists enforced through HTTP proxy, IP, or port-based controls' and 'limiting DNS resolution to designated trusted resolvers to avoid DNS-based exfiltration'. Control 2: 'Write operations must be blocked outside of the active workspace at an OS level' via 'enterprise-level policy that blocks any such operation on known-sensitive paths, regardless of whether or not the user manually approves the action.' Control 3 is the strongest form and matches the guidance's reading exactly: 'Application-specific configuration files, including those located within the current workspace, must be protected from any modification by the agent, with no user approval of such actions by the IDE possible', with the stated rationale that 'hooks and MCP initialization functions often run outside of a sandbox environment, offering an opportunity to escape sandbox controls.' Published 2026-01-30, author Rich Harang. Claim is not version_sensitive so the tier-3 registration is acceptable; note this is a vendor engineering blog rather than a standard, but the controls are corroborated structurally by the Claude Code defaults in claims 04, 02 and 08.

statement: Nasr et al., "The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections" (arXiv:2510.09023, submitted 2025-10-10), bypassed 12 recent defenses using gradient descent, reinforcement learning, random search and human-guided exploration, achieving attack success rates above 90% for most, while the majority of those defenses originally reported near-zero attack success rates.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; applies to detection- and training-based prompt-injection defenses evaluated on static benchmarks
candidate_guidance: This is the strongest available evidence for the repo's containment-over-detection stance. Any vendor or paper reporting near-zero ASR on a static benchmark should be treated as unvalidated until tested adaptively. Use this to set a repo rule: do not adopt a prompt-injection defense on the strength of its own benchmark number alone.

sources.title: [2510.09023] The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

reason: Confirmed against the arXiv primary. Title, ID and submission date (2025-10-10) all match; first author Milad Nasr. The abstract supports each quantitative element: 12 recent defenses bypassed, attack methodology spanning 'gradient descent, reinforcement learning, random search, and human-guided exploration', attack success rates 'above 90% for most', against defenses of which 'the majority... originally reported near-zero attack success rates'. The paper's own thesis — that static or computationally weak evaluations miss weaknesses that adaptive attackers with optimization budget expose — is precisely the inference the guidance draws, so the proposed repo rule (do not adopt a prompt-injection defense on the strength of its own benchmark number alone) is a faithful application rather than an extrapolation. This is the correct anchor for the bucket's containment-over-detection stance. Pair it with claim 15, which is the one piece of evidence pointing the other way for out-of-band enforcement specifically.

statement: PromptArmor (arXiv:2507.15219) reports both a false positive rate and a false negative rate below 1% on the AgentDojo benchmark when using off-the-shelf GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 or o4-mini as the guardrail LLM, by prompting the guardrail model to detect and remove injected prompts before the agent processes the input.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic filter-LLM defense pattern; benchmark result specific to AgentDojo and the named guardrail models
candidate_guidance: Record as a benchmark result, NOT as a deployable guarantee. PromptArmor is a detection-based in-band defense of exactly the class that arXiv:2510.09023 (claim 13) bypassed at >90% ASR under adaptive attack, and its numbers are static-benchmark numbers. The registered tier-5 playbook attributes this result to 'ICLR 2026' — that venue attribution is unverified (see open questions); cite the arXiv ID instead.

reason: Confirmed, but only after correcting my own first pass. An initial fetch summarised the guardrail models as 'o1-mini'; I re-fetched the v1 abstract for verbatim text and the paper does say o4-mini, matching the claim exactly: 'using GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, or o4-mini, PromptArmor achieves both a false positive rate and a false negative rate below 1% on the AgentDojo benchmark.' Submitted 2025-07-21. The mechanism description (prompting an off-the-shelf LLM to detect and remove injected prompts before the agent processes the input) matches. On the venue open question: an OpenReview forum does exist under the alternate title 'PromptArmor: An Essential Baseline for Prompt Injection Defenses' (id=IeNXtofK6T), submitted to ICLR 2026 with an initial submission date of 2025-09-14; the forum page itself is behind browser verification, so acceptance status remains unconfirmed. Submission is not acceptance — the guidance's instruction to cite the arXiv ID and not the venue stands and should not be relaxed. One nuance the guidance should absorb rather than contradict: the abstract does claim 'We also demonstrate PromptArmor's effectiveness against adaptive attacks', so the accurate framing is not that PromptArmor never tested adaptively, but that its adaptive testing is author-run and the sub-1% figures are static AgentDojo numbers — exactly the pattern claim 13 shows collapsing when an independent attacker with optimization budget moves second.

statement: "Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents" (arXiv:2606.26479, submitted 2026-06-25) evaluated out-of-band defenses including CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS and FORGE. Testing Progent on an open-weight Qwen2.5-7B agent, mean attack success fell from 25.8% to 4.2%, and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%). The authors characterise this as one small-scale data point and note a stronger optimized attack remains untested.
applicability: Vendor-agnostic; result specific to Progent on Qwen2.5-7B, not to the other named defenses
candidate_guidance: New since the 2026-07-12 baseline window and the most interesting counterweight to claim 13: deterministic out-of-band enforcement (capabilities, information-flow labels, reference monitors) may hold up adaptively where in-band detection did not. Log as a hypothesis with an explicit authors'-own caveat, not as a finding — the sample is one defense, one small open-weight model, one hand-crafted attack. Do not generalise to CaMeL/FIDES/RTBAS/FORGE, which were surveyed but not adaptively tested here.

sources.title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents (arXiv:2606.26479)

reason: Confirmed against the arXiv primary. Title and ID match; submitted 2026-06-25; authors Narisetty, Kore, Kattamanchi, Kumarapu. The five out-of-band defenses are named as claimed (CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, FORGE), and the numbers are exact: 'Progent cut mean attack success roughly sixfold (25.8% to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%).' The authors' own caveat is stronger than the claim renders it and should be carried in full: they call this 'one small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box attack template' and state that 'a stronger optimized (white-box GCG) attack remains open'. The paper also frames existing out-of-band evaluations as relying on static benchmarks 'similar to methodology that previously failed for in-band defenses', which makes it a deliberate companion to claim 13 rather than a contradiction of it. The guidance's handling is correct on both counts that matter: log as hypothesis not finding, and do not generalise to CaMeL/FIDES/RTBAS/FORGE, which are surveyed as representatives of the category but not adaptively tested here. Only Progent was empirically attacked, and only on Qwen2.5-7B.

statement: Microsoft's Semantic Kernel had two critical vulnerabilities enabling the prompt-injection-to-code-execution path. CVE-2026-26030 affects the semantic-kernel Python package prior to version 1.39.4: InMemoryVectorStore builds filter expressions as Python lambdas and executes them via eval(), so unsafe string interpolation of attacker-controlled vector-store fields yields RCE, escapable via object traversal (CWE-94, CVSS 9.9 Critical). CVE-2026-25592 affects the Semantic Kernel .NET SDK (Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Core) prior to version 1.71.0: SessionsPythonPlugin's DownloadFileAsync — and per NVD also UploadFileAsync — was accidentally annotated with the [KernelFunction] attribute and exposed as an AI-callable function without path validation, giving a path-traversal arbitrary-file-write primitive on the host that escaped the Azure Container Apps dynamic-session container isolation (CVSS 9.9 Critical). The CVEs were published 2026-02-06 (CVE-2026-25592) and 2026-02-19 (CVE-2026-26030); Microsoft's Security Blog analysis 'When prompts become shells' was published later, on 2026-05-07, and is an analysis write-up rather than the disclosure event.
applicability: Microsoft Semantic Kernel: Python <1.39.4, .NET SDK <1.71.0
candidate_guidance: Keep the substance: this is concrete proof that prompt injection reaches code execution through ordinary tool-surface bugs rather than exotic model attacks, and CVE-2026-25592's shape is the generalisable lesson — an over-broad tool annotation silently promoted an internal file-transfer helper into the model's action surface, and the write landed on the host rather than inside the container that was supposed to contain it. Audit which functions are exported to the model, and treat any tool that writes to the host filesystem as trifecta-relevant. Microsoft's stated principle is worth quoting: the LLM is not a security boundary, the tools you expose define the attacker's scope, and any tool parameter the model can influence must be treated as attacker-controlled input. Correct the dates when citing: patch-currency deadlines run from February 2026, not May. Any pinned Semantic Kernel dependency in the estate has been exposed for roughly five months longer than the registered date implies, so treat the version floors (Python >=1.39.4, .NET >=1.71.0) as overdue rather than recent. Note also that mitigation for the .NET issue is available without upgrading, via a Function Invocation Filter that allowlists file paths before execution.
